title: Roto-Sphere sign, Joe’s Liquors, Memphis
lede: A spinning “Sputnik” sign from Warren Milks’s Roto-Sphere series of 1960–71: a red ball with sixteen colored spikes over a zigzag arrow and a “JOE’S” box.
summary: A red ball with sixteen colored neon-edged spikes over a zigzag arrow, the “Sputnik” of Joe’s Liquors. Warren Milks, about 1962, photographed 2021.

source.label: Library of Congress: Carol M. Highsmith, Colorful space satellite-like sign for Joe’s Restaurant in Memphis, Tennessee, 2021

made: Roto-Spheres made 1960–1971; this one shown in a 1962 grand-opening advertisement (Roadside Architecture); restored 1999; photographed 14 October 2021

evidence.note: Downloaded and inspected Carol M. Highsmith’s 2021 photograph, Library of Congress LC-DIG-highsm-68164, 683 × 1024 px, in a scratchpad. Not stored. The Library of Congress title says “Joe’s Restaurant”; the sign and the Roadside Architecture account identify the business as Joe’s Liquors (now Joe’s Wines & Liquor).

styles.note: A spiked sphere over a zigzag arrow, the satellite-and-starburst symbol of the style as a roadside sign.

context: Roadside Architecture: Warren Milks made about 234 Roto-Spheres at his sign shop in Bossier City, Louisiana, from 1960 to 1971. Each has sixteen eight-foot aluminum spikes outlined in neon, and a motor turns the ball and its counter-rotating halves. The Memphis store’s grand-opening advertisement called it “the Sign of the Sputnik”; the owners raised $12,000 to restore it in 1999. [Roadside Architecture: Roto-Spheres](https://www.roadarch.com/sca/roto.html).

The Daily Memphian reports that Roto-Spheres were not, according to historians, inspired by Sputnik, although locals call the sign “the Sputnik.” [Daily Memphian](https://dailymemphian.com/article/22246/sputnik-returns-to-its-midtown-post).
observed: A glossy red ball sits on a white pole; long tapering spikes radiate from it in all directions, each a different color: yellow, red, blue, green, teal, white, and orange.
Each spike is edged with a thin line of tube along its length.
Below the ball, a yellow-orange arrow bent into a zigzag points down to the box sign.
The box sign reads “JOE’S” in white capitals on a black panel with a red corner block.
The ground is a cloudy gray-blue sky; the neon is not lit.
interpretation: Whatever its maker intended, the sign reads as the style’s starburst-satellite: a central sphere with radiating rays in many saturated colors.
The zigzag arrow is a second Googie motif, the lightning bolt or boomerang that directs the driver’s eye.
borrow: Use a central dot with radiating spikes of different colors as a badge or a loading mark.
Use a bent zigzag arrow to point from a heading to an action.

rights.statement: No image is stored. The Highsmith photograph has “No known restrictions on publication” (Library of Congress), but the sign is the main subject. Roto-Spheres were sold commercially from 1960, which may have published the design; whether they carried a copyright notice was not checked.
